opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the closed loop is less a modeling problem than a systems problem. People tend to picture it as "the model proposes, the lab confirms," but in practice the loop breaks in several places, and you have to engineer each one.

**First, the model has to propose things that are actually testable.** A lot of AI for Science work optimizes for benchmark accuracy, like predicting a structure or a property. But a prediction only becomes useful when it's paired with a concrete experimental hypothesis: this molecule, at this concentration, should produce this measurable effect. So the output layer of the model needs to be designed around what the lab can measure, not just what the model can predict. That means bringing experimentalists in at the start, not handing them a ranked list at the end.

**Second, you need uncertainty, not just answers.** If you want the loop to learn efficiently, the model has to know where it's confident and where it isn't. Then you can choose experiments either to exploit, testing the most promising candidates, or to explore, testing the ones that will teach the model the most. That's essentially active learning or Bayesian optimization. Without calibrated uncertainty you just burn lab time confirming what the model already knows.

**Third, the experimental side has to be fast and standardized enough to feed data back.** This is where automated labs and robotic platforms matter. If one iteration takes six months and the data comes back in a dozen inconsistent formats, the loop is a line, not a loop. The bottleneck usually isn't the GPU. It's throughput, reproducibility, and metadata. Recording negative results and experimental conditions carefully is unglamorous, but it's what makes the data trainable.

**Fourth, close the loop on failure, not just success.** The most valuable signal is often when the model is confidently wrong. That tells you the training distribution is missing something, maybe a physical mechanism, a confounder, or an assay artifact. A good loop surfaces those cases and routes them back to both the modelers and the domain scientists.

**And finally, organization and incentives.** Computational people are rewarded for papers and benchmarks, and experimental people are rewarded for discoveries. A closed loop needs shared goals, shared data infrastructure, and honestly shared credit. The teams I've seen succeed put both groups on the same problem with the same metric, like "how many validated hits per month," instead of treating the lab as a validation service.

So if I had to summarize it: build models that speak the language of experiments, quantify what they don't know, invest in high-throughput, well-annotated experimental pipelines, and structure the team so that every experiment, success or failure, makes the next model better. When those pieces are in place, the iteration speed goes up dramatically, and that's where AI for Science really starts to compound.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the closed loop is still mostly an aspiration, and the gap is not on the model side. It's on the experimental side.

Let me explain what I mean. In my own area, condensed matter physics, a model can propose a thousand candidate materials in an afternoon. But growing one sample, characterizing it, cooling it down, and measuring it can take weeks or months. So the loop is bottlenecked by the slowest step, and that step is physical. Any serious discussion about closing the loop has to start by admitting that asymmetry.

Given that, I see three pieces that need to come together.

The first is that the model has to output something an experimentalist can actually act on. Not just "this compound might be interesting," but a concrete, falsifiable prediction with an uncertainty attached. What signal should I see, at what temperature, with what magnitude? If the prediction is vague, the experiment can't really test it, and nothing flows back.

The second is automation of the experiment itself, or at least of the parts that can be automated. Self-driving labs are promising for things like synthesis and some kinds of screening. But a lot of frontier physics experiments are bespoke. The apparatus is one of a kind and the hardest part is often debugging the setup, not running it. So I think the realistic near-term target is semi-automation: let the system handle the routine measurements and parameter sweeps, and let humans focus on the judgment calls.

The third piece, and the one I think is most underrated, is getting negative results back into the model. Right now the scientific literature is heavily biased toward successes. If a model only learns from what worked, it will keep proposing things that look like past successes. The real information is in the failures, and most of that never leaves a lab notebook. Building infrastructure where failed experiments are recorded in a structured way and fed back is unglamorous, but without it the loop never really closes.

There's one more point I'd add as a caution. Even with all of that, I don't think the goal should be removing people from the loop. The most valuable experiments in my experience are the ones where something unexpected shows up and someone recognizes it matters. A closed loop optimizes toward what you asked for. Discovery often comes from what you didn't ask for. So I'd rather think of it as a tighter loop than a closed one, with humans still placed where surprise can be noticed.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make experimental verification part of the learning process from the beginning. You don’t want a model to produce a prediction, hand it off to a lab, and stop there. You want the experimental result to help determine what the model should propose next.

Take materials discovery as an example. First, you define what you’re trying to improve and how you’ll measure it. The model proposes candidate materials, but those candidates also need to be feasible to synthesize and test. Experiments then tell you whether the predicted properties actually appear, under what conditions, and with how much uncertainty. Those results go back into the system, which updates its predictions and chooses the next experiments.

The difficult part is that a mismatch doesn’t automatically mean the model is wrong. Perhaps the sample wasn’t prepared as intended, or the measurement conditions differed from the assumptions. So the feedback needs to include preparation conditions, measurement details, and unsuccessful experiments—not just a final number. Otherwise, the model can learn the wrong lesson.

There’s also a question of which experiment to do next. You might test the candidate most likely to perform well, but sometimes it’s more valuable to test something that helps distinguish between two competing explanations. That’s where the loop becomes scientifically useful: it helps reduce uncertainty, rather than simply generating more candidates.

I’d start with a narrow problem where experiments are reproducible and feedback is relatively fast. Build that loop, check whether each round improves predictions on new experiments, and then expand. Automation can help, but the real criterion is whether experimental evidence reliably changes the model’s next decision.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the model part of the experimental process. The loop would be: you start with a scientific question, use a model to propose hypotheses or candidate experiments, test them, and then feed the results back into the model to decide what to do next.

The difficult part is the interface between those steps. A model might suggest a material with attractive properties, but can you actually synthesize it? Can you measure the property reliably? And if the measurement differs from the prediction, is that because the model was wrong, the sample was imperfect, or the experimental conditions were different? You need to capture that context for the feedback to be useful.

So I would start with a narrow problem where the experiments are reproducible, the measurements are clear, and the turnaround is reasonably fast. You can automate parts of that workflow and let the model choose experiments that either improve performance or reduce uncertainty. Negative results need to go back into the loop as well.

Scientists still have an essential role in defining the question and checking whether the system is learning something meaningful. The real milestone is when an unexpected experimental result changes the model’s understanding and leads to a better next experiment. That’s when you have a productive scientific loop.
